ai_literacy.q: What is the key difference between Discriminative and Generative models?
options: Discriminative models learn P(y|x); Generative models learn P(x,y)
Discriminative models generate data; Generative models classify
Discriminative are unsupervised; Generative are supervised
ai_literacy.exp: Discriminative models learn conditional probability P(y|x). Generative models learn the joint distribution P(x,y) and can generate new samples.

ai_literacy.q: Tokenization in Large Language Models (LLMs) refers to:
options: Breaking input text into smaller units (words/subwords/chars)
The process of fine-tuning a model
ai_literacy.exp: Tokenization breaks text into tokens (subwords, words, characters) before feeding to the LLM.

ai_literacy.q: Zero-shot prompting means:
options: Providing many examples in the prompt
Asking the model to perform a task without any examples
Running the model with no GPU
ai_literacy.exp: Zero-shot asks the LLM to perform tasks without prior examples, relying on pre-trained knowledge.

ai_literacy.q: In RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation), the retriever's role is to:
options: Fetch relevant documents from external knowledge bases
ai_literacy.exp: The retriever fetches semantically relevant documents from external databases, providing the LLM with up-to-date context.

ai_literacy.q: LLM 'hallucination' refers to:
options: The model running out of memory
Generating confidently stated but factually incorrect output
ai_literacy.exp: Hallucination is when LLMs produce plausible-sounding but fabricated or incorrect information.

ai_literacy.q: Embedding spaces in NLP represent:
options: High-dimensional vector space where similar tokens are close
ai_literacy.exp: Embedding spaces map words to vectors where semantic similarity corresponds to geometric proximity.

ai_literacy.q: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting encourages LLMs to:
ai_literacy.exp: CoT prompting includes intermediate reasoning steps, guiding the model to think through complex problems systematically.

ai_literacy.q: Few-shot prompting involves:
options: Providing a small number of examples in the prompt
ai_literacy.exp: Few-shot prompting provides worked examples in the prompt to guide the model's output format and behavior.

ai_literacy.q: Bias mitigation in Responsible AI aims to:
options: Reduce unfair discrimination based on protected attributes
ai_literacy.exp: Bias mitigation detects and reduces discriminatory patterns in AI related to race, gender, religion, etc.

ai_literacy.q: Multi-modal LLMs differ from text-only models because they:
options: Can process text, images, audio and other modalities
ai_literacy.exp: Multi-modal LLMs process and generate multiple data types (text, image, audio) unlike single-modality models.

ai_literacy.q: Neural network scaling laws state performance improves with:
options: Increasing parameters, data, and compute together
ai_literacy.exp: Kaplan et al.'s scaling laws show LLM performance improves predictably as parameters, data, and compute scale together.

ai_literacy.q: RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback) is used to:
options: Align model outputs with human preferences and reduce toxicity
ai_literacy.exp: RLHF uses human ratings to train a reward model, then fine-tunes the LLM to produce more helpful and harmless outputs.

ai_literacy.q: What is a 'knowledge graph' in the context of RAG?
options: A structured representation of entities and their relationships
ai_literacy.exp: A knowledge graph represents real-world entities (nodes) connected by typed relationships (edges), enabling rich semantic querying.

ai_literacy.q: Data privacy in AI is a concern because:
options: Training data may contain memorized personal information (PII)
ai_literacy.exp: LLMs trained on web-scale data may memorize and regurgitate personal information from training datasets.

ai_literacy.q: The 'temperature' parameter in LLM generation controls:
options: Randomness/creativity of outputs — higher = more random
ai_literacy.exp: Temperature controls sampling randomness: low temperature = deterministic/conservative; high temperature = creative/diverse outputs.

ai_literacy.q: What is the Self-Attention mechanism in Transformer models?
options: A mechanism where the model focuses on its own weights only
Computes attention weights between all pairs of tokens in an input sequence simultaneously
A method to reduce token count
ai_literacy.exp: Self-attention allows each token in a sequence to dynamically attend to and weigh the context of all other tokens, capturing long-range dependencies.

ai_literacy.q: In Vector Databases, what does HNSW stand for?
options: Hierarchical Navigable Small World — an approximate nearest neighbor graph index
ai_literacy.exp: HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) is a graph-based indexing algorithm providing logarithmic search time for vector nearest neighbors.

ai_literacy.q: What is a 'Prompt Injection' attack in LLM applications?
options: Crashing the GPU with malformed tokens
Manipulating user inputs to override system prompt instructions and bypass guardrails
Injecting SQL queries into a relational database
ai_literacy.exp: Prompt injection occurs when untrusted user input tricks the LLM into disregarding original developer instructions, adopting new malicious personas or leaking system secrets.

ai_literacy.q: Fine-Tuning vs RAG — which is best for accessing dynamically changing real-time data?
ai_literacy.exp: RAG is superior for rapidly changing or real-time data because it retrieves current documents without requiring expensive model retraining or fine-tuning.

ai_literacy.q: What is the primary role of LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) in LLM fine-tuning?
options: Freezing base model weights and training small low-rank decomposition matrices, reducing memory usage
ai_literacy.exp: LoRA freezes the pre-trained model weights and injects trainable rank decomposition matrices into each transformer layer, drastically cutting GPU VRAM requirements.

ai_literacy.q: Cosine Similarity between two identical normalized vectors equals:
ai_literacy.exp: Cosine similarity measures cos(θ). For identical vectors, θ=0°, so cos(0°)=1. Orthogonal vectors have similarity 0.

ai_literacy.q: What is the 'Needle in a Haystack' test used for in LLM benchmarking?
options: Testing an LLM's ability to recall specific facts placed at arbitrary positions in large context windows
ai_literacy.exp: The Needle in a Haystack test evaluates retrieval accuracy across various depth percentages of an LLM's full context window.

ai_literacy.q: Top-P (Nucleus Sampling) set to 0.1 means:
options: The model only considers tokens comprising top 10% of cumulative probability mass
ai_literacy.exp: Top-P=0.1 restricts token sampling strictly to the tight pool of most likely tokens whose cumulative probability is 10%, producing highly focused outputs.

ai_literacy.q: What is 'model quantization' (e.g. INT8, 4-bit AWQ)?
options: Reducing weight precision from 16-bit float to lower bit integers (INT8/4-bit) to reduce memory and latency
ai_literacy.exp: Quantization compresses model weights into lower-precision formats (like INT8 or 4-bit), significantly reducing VRAM footprint and accelerating inference with minimal accuracy drop.

ai_literacy.q: What is the difference between BERT and GPT architectural styles?
options: BERT is Decoder-only; GPT is Encoder-only
BERT is Encoder-only (bidirectional context); GPT is Decoder-only (autoregressive next-token prediction)
ai_literacy.exp: BERT uses Transformer encoders to look at both left and right context (ideal for classification). GPT uses Transformer decoders for causal, autoregressive generation.

ai_literacy.q: In Responsible AI, what does 'Demographic Parity' evaluate?
options: Equal acceptance/positive prediction rates across different protected demographic groups
Number of tokens used per dialect
ai_literacy.exp: Demographic Parity is a fairness metric requiring that the proportion of positive decisions is equal across protected subgroups (e.g., gender, ethnicity).

ai_literacy.q: What is 'Chain-of-Verification' (CoVe) in LLM generation?
options: Having the model draft responses, generate verification questions, check them independently, and revise the final answer
ai_literacy.exp: Chain-of-Verification (CoVe) mitigates hallucinations by having the LLM generate verification questions to fact-check its own draft before producing the verified response.

ai_literacy.q: What is a Vector Embedding dimension?
options: The file size of the database
The length of the floating-point coordinate array representing semantic meaning (e.g. 1536 floats)
ai_literacy.exp: The embedding dimension represents the size of the numerical coordinate vector (e.g., 768 or 1536) used to encode the semantic features of a text chunk.

ai_literacy.q: What is 'RLAIF' (Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback)?
options: Using a larger, stronger AI model to evaluate and provide reward labels instead of human annotators
ai_literacy.exp: RLAIF (Constitutional AI) uses an AI evaluator to provide feedback and preference labels, replacing costly human annotator loops in RLHF.

ai_literacy.q: What causes 'Catastrophic Forgetting' in neural networks?
options: Fine-tuning heavily on a new domain causes the network to lose performance on previously learned general knowledge
ai_literacy.exp: Catastrophic forgetting occurs when a neural network overwrites previously acquired knowledge while training on new, narrow datasets.

At least once before checking condition

pseudocode.q: What does a 'static' local variable do?
options: Preserves its value across function calls
pseudocode.exp: Static local variables are initialized once and retain their value between successive function calls.

pseudocode.q: What is the output of: print(12 >> 2)?

pseudocode.q: What is ~5 (bitwise NOT of 5) in Python?
pseudocode.exp: Bitwise NOT flips all bits. ~5 = -(5+1) = -6 in Python's two's complement representation.

pseudocode.q: What does `(n & (n - 1)) == 0` check for a positive integer n?
options: Whether n is a power of 2
Whether n is a prime number

pseudocode.q: What does Brian Kernighan's algorithm `n = n & (n - 1)` do inside a loop?
options: Clears the lowest set bit of n, counting set bits
pseudocode.exp: Each iteration of n = n & (n - 1) turns off the rightmost set bit, counting the number of set bits in O(number of set bits) time.

pseudocode.q: What is the value of `7 % -3` in C/C++?
pseudocode.exp: In C99 and later, the sign of the remainder matches the dividend: 7 = (-3)*(-2) + 1. So 7 % -3 = 1.

pseudocode.exp: 2 is 010₂ and 3 is 011₂. XOR: 010 ^ 011 = 001₂ = 1. (Note: ^ is bitwise XOR, not exponentiation!).

dsa.q: Time complexity of Binary Search:
dsa.exp: Binary search halves search space each iteration → O(log n).

dsa.q: Which data structure follows LIFO?
dsa.exp: Stack is Last-In-First-Out.

dsa.q: In a BST, where is the maximum element?
dsa.exp: BST property: right children > parent, so rightmost node is the maximum.

dsa.q: Which sorting algorithm has best-case O(n)?
dsa.exp: Insertion Sort is O(n) best-case on already sorted arrays.

dsa.q: Time complexity of Merge Sort:
dsa.exp: Merge Sort always divides in half (log n levels) and merges in O(n) per level = O(n log n).

dsa.q: In a circular linked list, the last node points to:
dsa.exp: In circular linked list, last node's next pointer points back to the head (first node).

dsa.q: Queue follows which order?
dsa.exp: Queue is First-In-First-Out (FIFO).

dsa.q: Inorder traversal of a BST produces:
dsa.exp: BST inorder traversal (Left→Root→Right) visits nodes in ascending sorted order.

dsa.q: Average-case complexity of Quick Sort:
dsa.exp: Quick Sort averages O(n log n) when pivots create balanced partitions.

dsa.q: A singly linked list node contains:
dsa.exp: Singly linked list node has data and one 'next' pointer to the next node.

dsa.q: How do you detect a cycle in a singly linked list in O(1) space?
options: Use a hash table of visited nodes
Floyd's Tortoise and Hare algorithm (slow and fast pointers)
dsa.exp: Floyd's cycle-finding algorithm moves slow pointer by 1 step and fast pointer by 2 steps. If there is a cycle, they meet in O(N) time and O(1) memory.

dsa.q: What is the minimum number of queues needed to implement a Stack?
dsa.exp: Two queues can implement a stack by transferring elements to maintain LIFO ordering on push/pop operations.

dsa.q: Height of a balanced AVL tree with N nodes is:
dsa.exp: AVL trees maintain a balance factor of -1, 0, or +1 at every node, ensuring strictly logarithmic height O(log N).

dsa.q: Which graph traversal uses a Queue data structure?
dsa.exp: Breadth-First Search (BFS) explores vertices level-by-level using a FIFO Queue.

dsa.q: Topological Sort can be performed on which type of graph?
dsa.exp: Topological Sort orders vertices such that for every directed edge u→v, u comes before v. This is only possible on Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs).

dsa.q: Time complexity of Dijkstra's algorithm using a Min-Priority Queue (Binary Heap):
dsa.exp: With a binary heap, extracting min takes O(log V) for V vertices, and decrease-key takes O(log V) for E edges → O((V + E) log V).

dsa.q: What is the time complexity of building a heap (Heapify) of N elements from an arbitrary array?
dsa.exp: Building a heap using bottom-up heapify takes linear O(N) time because lower levels with more nodes have smaller heights.

dsa.q: What is the recurrence relation for the 0/1 Knapsack problem with capacity W and item i?
dsa.exp: For 0/1 Knapsack, either exclude item i: dp[i-1][w], or include item i: val[i] + dp[i-1][w - wt[i]], taking the maximum of both choices.

dsa.q: In a Hash Table with open addressing, what is 'quadratic probing'?
options: Using a linked list at each bucket
Resolving collisions using h(k, i) = (h'(k) + c1*i + c2*i²) mod m
dsa.exp: Quadratic probing avoids primary clustering by using a quadratic polynomial of the collision step i to compute the next probe index.

dsa.q: What is the worst-case time complexity of Quick Sort?
dsa.exp: When the pivot chosen is always the smallest or largest element (e.g., already sorted array with naive first/last element pivot), Quick Sort degrades to O(N²).

dsa.q: To find the middle element of a linked list in a single pass, you should use:
options: Two pointers: one advancing 1 step, one advancing 2 steps
dsa.exp: Fast and slow pointer technique: when fast pointer reaches the end (moves 2x), slow pointer is exactly at the midpoint.

dsa.q: The Two-Pointer approach to find two numbers summing to a target requires the array to be:
options: Sorted in ascending or descending order
dsa.exp: The two-pointer technique (left at 0, right at n-1) relies on monotonicity of a sorted array to decide whether to increment left or decrement right.

dsa.q: What is the diameter of a Binary Tree?
options: The length of the longest path between any two nodes in a tree
The depth of the root node
dsa.exp: The diameter (or width) of a binary tree is the number of nodes (or edges) on the longest path between any two arbitrary nodes in the tree.

dsa.q: Postorder traversal of a binary tree visits nodes in which sequence?
dsa.exp: Postorder traversal processes the left subtree, then the right subtree, and finally the root node (Left → Right → Root).

dsa.q: A complete binary tree with N nodes has height:
dsa.exp: In a complete binary tree, all levels except possibly the last are completely filled, resulting in height floor(log2(N)).

dbms.q: Which normal form eliminates partial dependencies?
dbms.exp: 2NF removes partial dependencies — non-key attributes depending on part of a composite PK.

dbms.q: INNER JOIN returns:
options: Only matching rows from both tables
dbms.exp: INNER JOIN returns only rows with matching values in both tables.

dbms.q: A foreign key ensures:
dbms.exp: Foreign key enforces referential integrity — child table values must exist in parent table's primary key.

dbms.q: HAVING clause is used to:
dbms.exp: HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY, unlike WHERE which filters rows before grouping.

dbms.q: 1NF requires:
options: No repeating groups; all atomic values
dbms.exp: 1NF: each cell contains a single atomic value; no repeating groups.

dbms.q: Which SQL command grants access privileges?
dbms.exp: GRANT is a DCL command for giving users database access privileges.

dbms.q: LEFT JOIN returns:
dbms.exp: LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table plus matched rows from right (NULLs for no match).

dbms.q: ACID stands for:
dbms.exp: ACID: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability — properties ensuring reliable transactions.

dbms.q: Which SQL function counts rows including NULLs?
dbms.exp: COUNT(*) counts all rows including those with NULL values, unlike COUNT(column) which skips NULLs.

dbms.q: 3NF eliminates:
dbms.exp: 3NF eliminates transitive dependencies — non-key attributes depending on other non-key attributes.

dbms.q: A table is in Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF) if and only if:
options: For every functional dependency X → Y, X is a superkey
It has no composite primary keys
dbms.exp: BCNF is a stricter version of 3NF: for every non-trivial functional dependency X → Y, the determinant X must be a superkey.

dbms.q: What is a 'Dirty Read' in database transactions?
options: Reading data corrupted by disk failure
A transaction reads uncommitted changes made by another concurrent transaction
dbms.exp: A dirty read occurs when Transaction A modifies a row without committing, and Transaction B reads that uncommitted modified data (which might later be rolled back).

dbms.q: Which transaction isolation level prevents Dirty Reads, Non-Repeatable Reads, and Phantom Reads?
dbms.exp: Serializable is the highest isolation level; it completely executes concurrent transactions as if they were executed sequentially, preventing all read anomalies.

dbms.q: Difference between `UNION` and `UNION ALL` in SQL:
options: UNION ALL removes duplicates; UNION keeps all
UNION removes duplicate rows; UNION ALL retains all rows including duplicates
dbms.exp: UNION performs an implicit distinct sort operation to eliminate duplicates across result sets. UNION ALL simply concatenates sets without deduplication, making it faster.

dbms.q: What is a Clustered Index in relational databases?
options: An index created on secondary foreign keys
An index that dictates the physical storage order of rows in the table (only 1 per table)
An index stored on disk partition
A temporary index created in memory
dbms.exp: A clustered index determines the physical order of data pages on disk. Since data can only be physically stored in one order, a table can have only one clustered index.

dbms.q: In SQL, what does `ON DELETE CASCADE` on a Foreign Key do?
options: Automatically deletes matching child table rows when the referenced parent row is deleted
dbms.exp: ON DELETE CASCADE ensures referential integrity by automatically propagating row deletions from the primary key table to all referencing foreign key rows.

dbms.q: What is the purpose of Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)?
options: To write log files for analytics
To ensure transaction changes are written to append-only log on disk before being applied to data pages, ensuring Durability
dbms.exp: WAL guarantees the 'D' (Durability) in ACID: transaction logs are flushed to persistent disk before memory changes are written to database tables, enabling crash recovery.

dbms.q: Which SQL window function assigns a unique sequential integer to each row without gaps?
dbms.exp: ROW_NUMBER() assigns a continuous unique sequential integer (1, 2, 3...) to rows within a partition regardless of ties. RANK leaves gaps for ties; DENSE_RANK ties without gaps.

dbms.q: What does the CAP theorem state regarding distributed databases?
options: Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance cannot all be guaranteed simultaneously in a network partition
Databases must use C++, Assembly, and Python
All distributed databases are ACID compliant
Queries must execute in constant time
dbms.exp: CAP theorem (Brewer's theorem): in the presence of a network partition, a distributed system can guarantee either Consistency (CP) or Availability (AP), but not both.

dbms.q: What type of JOIN is needed to find an employee's manager in a single Employees table?
options: Self JOIN (joining table with itself on ManagerID = EmployeeID)
dbms.exp: A Self JOIN joins a table to itself using aliases (e.g. `FROM Employees e JOIN Employees m ON e.ManagerId = m.EmpId`) to model hierarchical relationships.

dbms.q: What is a Materialized View compared to a standard View?
options: A view whose query result is physically computed and stored on disk, refreshing periodically
A view that cannot be dropped
dbms.exp: A standard view is a saved virtual query recomputed on access. A Materialized View physically caches the query results on disk, drastically accelerating complex aggregation queries.

dbms.q: In 2-Phase Locking (2PL), what are the two phases?
options: Growing Phase (locks acquired, none released) and Shrinking Phase (locks released, none acquired)
dbms.exp: 2PL ensures serializability: During the Growing phase, transactions only acquire locks. Once a lock is released, the Shrinking phase begins and no new locks may be acquired.

dbms.q: Which SQL clause specifies the grouping condition that aggregates must satisfy?
dbms.exp: HAVING filters aggregated groups (e.g. `HAVING COUNT(*) > 5`). WHERE filters individual rows before grouping occurs.

dbms.q: What is an index seek vs an index scan?
options: Index Seek navigates the B-Tree directly to locate specific keys; Index Scan reads through the entire index page leaf chain
Index Scan only works on primary keys
dbms.exp: Index Seek uses the B-Tree hierarchy to jump directly to specific matching rows (O(log N)). Index Scan traverses all index leaf pages sequentially (O(N)).

dbms.q: What does `NULL = NULL` evaluate to in SQL standard three-valued logic?
dbms.exp: In SQL's three-valued logic, NULL represents an unknown value. Comparing two unknown values (`NULL = NULL`) evaluates to UNKNOWN (not TRUE). Use `IS NULL` instead.

oops.q: Multiple Inheritance allows:
options: Single class inheriting from one parent
A class inheriting from multiple parents
oops.exp: Multiple inheritance allows a class to inherit from more than one base class.

oops.q: Method overloading is:
oops.exp: Method overloading (same name, different parameters) is resolved at compile time.

oops.q: The 'super' keyword accesses:
oops.exp: 'super' refers to the immediate parent class for accessing constructors, methods, and attributes.

oops.q: Encapsulation bundles:
options: Data and methods together, with restricted access
oops.exp: Encapsulation combines data and methods in a class while restricting direct access to internals.

oops.q: Method overriding is:
oops.exp: Method overriding (redefining parent method in child class) is resolved at runtime based on actual object type.

oops.q: An abstract class can:
options: Have both abstract and concrete methods
oops.exp: Abstract classes can contain both abstract methods (no body) and fully implemented concrete methods.

oops.q: 'this' keyword refers to:
oops.exp: 'this' refers to the current object instance within a class method or constructor.

oops.q: Hierarchical inheritance means:
options: Many children inherit from one parent
oops.exp: Hierarchical inheritance: multiple child classes inherit from a single parent class.

oops.q: What principle says 'program to an interface, not an implementation'?
oops.exp: The Dependency Inversion Principle (D in SOLID) states high-level modules should depend on abstractions, not concrete implementations.

oops.q: Runtime polymorphism is achieved through:
oops.exp: Runtime polymorphism requires method overriding combined with inheritance, resolved via dynamic dispatch at runtime.

oops.q: How does C++ resolve the 'Diamond Problem' in multiple inheritance?
options: Using virtual base classes (e.g. `class B : virtual public A`)
oops.exp: Virtual base classes ensure that only one copy of the common grandparent class subobject is inherited by the grandchild, resolving ambiguity in multiple inheritance.

oops.q: Why should base class destructors be declared 'virtual' in C++?
options: To ensure the derived class destructor is called when deleting an object through a base class pointer
oops.exp: If a base class destructor is non-virtual, deleting a derived class object through a base pointer results in undefined behavior (only the base destructor runs, leaking derived resources).

oops.q: What is the difference between a Shallow Copy and a Deep Copy?
options: Shallow copy copies dynamically allocated heap memory; Deep copy copies pointers
Shallow copy duplicates pointer addresses (sharing memory); Deep copy allocates fresh memory and copies actual data
oops.exp: Shallow copy copies member values directly (meaning both objects point to the same heap buffer, causing double-free crashes). Deep copy allocates independent memory and duplicates values.

oops.q: What does the 'O' in SOLID design principles stand for?
options: Open/Closed Principle — software entities should be open for extension, but closed for modification
oops.exp: Open/Closed Principle states that classes should be designable so new behavior can be added (extension via inheritance/interfaces) without editing tested existing source code.

oops.q: What does the Liskov Substitution Principle (L in SOLID) state?
options: Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without altering program correctness
All classes must inherit from Object
Interfaces must have only one method
oops.exp: LSP: objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of a subclass without breaking application behavior or violating pre/post-conditions.

oops.q: What does Interface Segregation Principle (I in SOLID) advocate?
options: Combining all interfaces into one master interface
Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use (prefer small, role-specific interfaces)
oops.exp: ISP states that large 'fat' interfaces should be broken down into smaller, highly cohesive role interfaces so implementers only write what they need.

oops.q: In the Singleton Design Pattern, the constructor must be:
oops.exp: The constructor of a Singleton class must be private to prevent external instantiation with `new`, ensuring only one instance is created via `getInstance()`.

oops.q: What is the Factory Method Pattern?
options: A pattern where objects are manufactured in hardware
A creational pattern that provides an interface for creating objects in a superclass, letting subclasses alter the type of objects created
oops.exp: Factory Method delegates the instantiation logic to specialized factory methods or subclasses, decoupling caller code from concrete product classes.

oops.q: Why is 'Composition over Inheritance' generally preferred in enterprise design?
options: Composition provides greater runtime flexibility, avoids fragile base-class problems, and reduces tight coupling
oops.exp: HAS-A (composition) is looser coupled and lets you change component behaviors dynamically at runtime, avoiding the rigid compile-time coupling of IS-A (inheritance).

oops.q: In Java, what does the `final` keyword signify when applied to a class?
options: The class cannot be subclassed/extended (no inheritance allowed)
The class is deleted on JVM exit
oops.exp: A `final` class cannot be extended by any other class (e.g. `java.lang.String` is final for security and immutability guarantees).

oops.q: What is a Pure Virtual Function in C++?
options: A function with no return type
A virtual function with `= 0` in its declaration, making the class an abstract class
oops.exp: A pure virtual function (`virtual void draw() = 0;`) has no implementation in the base class and mandates that derived classes must provide an implementation.

oops.q: Can a constructor be declared `virtual` in C++?
options: No, constructors cannot be virtual because the vtable pointer is initialized inside the constructor itself
oops.exp: Constructors cannot be virtual because at the moment of construction, the object's type and its vpointer have not yet been fully set up.

oops.q: What is a Friend Function in C++?
options: A non-member function granted private and protected access to a class via the `friend` keyword
oops.exp: Declaring a function as `friend` inside a class definition grants that external non-member function access to all private and protected members of the class.

oops.q: What is 'method hiding' in object-oriented programming?
options: A subclass defines a static method with the same signature as a static method in the superclass, hiding it without overriding
oops.exp: Static methods cannot be overridden dynamically; when a derived class redefines a static method with identical signature, it hides the base method (resolved at compile time).

oops.q: What are 'Covariant Return Types' in method overriding?
options: An overriding method in a child class can return a more specific derived subtype of the return type declared in the parent method
oops.exp: Covariant return typing allows an overriding method to return a subtype of the superclass method's return type (e.g. parent returns `Animal`, child returns `Dog`).

os.q: Round Robin scheduling assigns:
options: Fixed time quantum in cyclic order
os.exp: Round Robin gives each process a fixed time quantum cyclically, ensuring fair CPU sharing.

os.q: Banker's Algorithm is used for:
os.exp: Banker's Algorithm avoids deadlock by checking if resource allocation leaves the system in a safe state.

os.q: A page fault occurs when:
options: Requested page is not in physical memory
os.exp: Page fault: accessed virtual page is not currently loaded in physical RAM, requiring OS to load it from disk.

os.q: FCFS scheduling suffers from:
os.exp: FCFS causes the convoy effect — short processes waiting behind long ones, reducing efficiency.

os.q: Thrashing occurs when:
options: Processes spend more time swapping pages than executing
os.exp: Thrashing: too many processes compete for limited frames, causing excessive page faults that degrade CPU utilization.

os.q: Which condition is NOT required for deadlock?
os.exp: Deadlock requires: Mutual Exclusion, Hold & Wait, No Preemption, and Circular Wait. CPU Scheduling is not one of them.

os.q: A semaphore is used for:
os.exp: Semaphores are integer-based synchronization primitives used to control access to shared resources and prevent race conditions.

os.q: Virtual memory allows:
options: Running programs larger than physical RAM by using disk as extension
os.exp: Virtual memory uses disk (swap space) to extend the apparent RAM, allowing programs larger than physical RAM to run.

os.q: The PCB (Process Control Block) stores:
options: All process state — registers, PC, memory maps, PID
os.exp: PCB holds the entire process state: PID, program counter, CPU registers, memory limits, I/O status, and scheduling info.

os.q: SJF (Shortest Job First) minimizes:
os.exp: SJF schedules the process with shortest burst time next, minimizing average waiting time — optimal for batch processing.

os.q: In context switching, the OS saves and restores:
options: PCB including all registers and memory state
os.exp: Context switch saves the full PCB of current process and loads PCB of next process, enabling multitasking.

os.q: LRU (Least Recently Used) is a:
os.exp: LRU is a page replacement policy: when a page frame is needed, evict the page that was least recently accessed.

os.q: What is a zombie process?
options: A process that has finished but whose exit status hasn't been collected by parent
os.exp: Zombie: process has finished execution but remains in process table until its parent reads its exit status via wait().

os.q: Segmentation fault (SIGSEGV) occurs when:
options: A process accesses memory outside its allocated segment
os.exp: SIGSEGV: process tried to access invalid memory — null pointer dereference, stack overflow, or out-of-bounds array access.

os.q: The OS kernel runs in which CPU mode?
options: Kernel/Supervisor mode with full hardware access
os.exp: Kernel mode has unrestricted hardware access. User programs run in user mode with restricted access to prevent system corruption.

os.q: What is Belady's Anomaly in operating systems?
options: LRU causes more page faults with more frames
FIFO page replacement can produce MORE page faults when physical page frames are increased
Optimal replacement is slower than FIFO
Disk access is faster than RAM
os.exp: Belady's Anomaly: In FIFO page replacement, allocating more memory page frames can counter-intuitively result in an increased number of page faults.

os.q: How many child processes are created if `fork()` is called 3 times consecutively?
os.exp: Formula for number of child processes created is 2^n - 1. For n=3 fork() calls, 2^3 - 1 = 7 child processes are created (8 processes in total including parent).

os.q: What is the key difference between a Mutex and a Binary Semaphore?
options: Mutex has ownership semantics (only the thread that locked it can unlock it); semaphore can be signaled by any thread
Mutex cannot be used in multithreading
os.exp: A Mutex enforces thread ownership — only the acquiring thread can release it. A binary semaphore is a signaling mechanism where any thread can signal/post.

os.q: Which three criteria MUST be satisfied to solve the Critical Section problem?
os.exp: Any valid solution to the critical section problem must satisfy: 1) Mutual Exclusion, 2) Progress, and 3) Bounded Waiting.

os.q: What is an 'Orphan Process' in Unix/Linux?
options: A child process whose parent terminated before calling wait(), adopted by init/systemd (PID 1)
os.exp: When a parent process terminates before its child, the child becomes an orphan and is immediately adopted by the init process (PID 1), which reaps its exit code.

os.q: Starvation differs from Deadlock because in Starvation:
options: A process is indefinitely delayed waiting for a resource while other processes continue making progress
os.exp: In deadlock, two or more processes are mutually blocked forever with zero progress. In starvation, the system continues running, but an unlucky low-priority process is perpetually postponed.

os.q: What is the primary role of the Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB)?
options: High-speed hardware cache for virtual-to-physical address translations to accelerate paging
os.exp: The TLB is an associative hardware cache in the MMU that stores recent virtual-to-physical page table mappings, avoiding double memory access penalties.

os.q: Which disk scheduling algorithm behaves like an elevator, servicing requests in one direction then reversing?
os.exp: SCAN (Elevator algorithm) sweeps the disk arm from one end to the other, servicing all requests along the path, then reverses direction at the boundary.

os.q: What is Internal Fragmentation in memory management?
options: Wasted memory space inside an allocated fixed-size block/page
os.exp: Internal fragmentation occurs when memory is allocated in fixed-size blocks (like pages) and the requested process size is smaller than the block size.

os.q: Paging eliminates which type of memory fragmentation completely?
os.exp: Because physical memory is divided into uniform fixed-size frames, any free frame can be allocated to any process, eliminating External Fragmentation.

networks.q: Which OSI layer handles end-to-end communication?
networks.exp: Transport Layer (Layer 4) provides end-to-end communication, error recovery, and flow control (TCP/UDP).

networks.q: IPv4 addresses are:
networks.exp: IPv4 = 32 bits (4 octets). IPv6 = 128 bits.

networks.q: TCP vs UDP — TCP is:
networks.exp: TCP uses three-way handshake, provides ordered reliable delivery with acknowledgements and retransmission.

networks.q: IP addressing and routing are handled by which OSI layer?
networks.exp: Network Layer (Layer 3) handles logical IP addressing and packet routing across networks.

networks.q: DNS operates at which OSI layer?
networks.exp: DNS is an Application Layer (Layer 7) protocol resolving domain names to IP addresses.

networks.q: TCP three-way handshake sequence is:
networks.exp: TCP connection starts: Client sends SYN → Server responds SYN-ACK → Client sends ACK. Connection established.

networks.q: HTTP status code 404 means:
networks.exp: 404 Not Found: the server cannot locate the requested resource at the given URL.

networks.q: HTTPS uses which protocol to encrypt traffic?
networks.exp: HTTPS = HTTP over TLS (Transport Layer Security), formerly SSL. TLS encrypts data in transit.

networks.q: ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) resolves:
networks.exp: ARP maps known IP addresses to physical MAC addresses on a local network segment.

networks.q: Which port does HTTPS use by default?
networks.exp: HTTPS uses port 443. HTTP uses port 80. SSH uses port 22. FTP uses port 21.

networks.q: A subnet mask /24 means:
options: First 24 bits are network, last 8 are hosts
networks.exp: /24 = 255.255.255.0. First 24 bits = network address, last 8 bits = host addresses (254 usable hosts).

networks.q: Firewall operates at which OSI layer primarily?
networks.exp: Firewalls inspect Network (IP) and Transport (TCP/UDP port) layer headers. Next-gen firewalls also inspect Application layer.

networks.q: Which protocol sends email FROM client to server?
networks.exp: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) sends outgoing email. POP3/IMAP are used to retrieve email from a server.

networks.q: Load balancer distributes requests to:
options: Multiple backend servers to prevent overload
networks.exp: Load balancers distribute incoming traffic across multiple backend server instances for high availability and horizontal scaling.

networks.q: The difference between LAN and WAN:
options: LAN is wireless; WAN is wired
LAN covers small area (building); WAN covers large area (country/globe)
LAN uses IP; WAN uses MAC
networks.exp: LAN (Local Area Network) covers small areas like offices. WAN (Wide Area Network) spans cities/countries — the Internet is a WAN.

networks.q: How many usable host IP addresses are available in a `/27` IPv4 subnet?
networks.exp: Host bits = 32 - 27 = 5 bits. Total IPs = 2^5 = 32. Subtracting network ID and broadcast address gives 32 - 2 = 30 usable host addresses.

networks.q: In TCP connection termination, how many packets are exchanged in a normal graceful close?
networks.exp: Graceful TCP closing is a 4-way handshake: Client sends FIN → Server sends ACK; Server sends FIN → Client sends ACK.

networks.q: Which phase of TCP Congestion Control doubles the Congestion Window (cwnd) every RTT?
networks.exp: During Slow Start, cwnd starts at 1 MSS and increments exponentially (doubles every Round Trip Time) until reaching ssthresh.

networks.q: Which IPv4 address block is designated as a Private Address Range (RFC 1918)?
networks.exp: RFC 1918 private ranges are: 10.0.0.0/8 (Class A), 172.16.0.0/12 (Class B), and 192.168.0.0/16 (Class C).

networks.q: How does TLS/HTTPS leverage asymmetric and symmetric cryptography together?
options: Asymmetric cryptography (RSA/ECC) establishes identity and securely exchanges a symmetric session key; symmetric (AES) encrypts bulk data
networks.exp: Asymmetric encryption is computationally expensive, so TLS uses it only for handshake authentication and key exchange, then switches to fast symmetric encryption (e.g. AES-GCM) for data transfer.

networks.q: What HTTP method is sent as a Preflight Request in Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)?
networks.exp: Browsers automatically dispatch a preflight HTTP `OPTIONS` request to check CORS permissions before sending non-simple cross-origin requests.

networks.q: What is the four-step handshake sequence used by DHCP to allocate an IP address?
networks.exp: DHCP uses the DORA sequence: Client broadcasts Discover → Server sends Offer → Client broadcasts Request → Server returns Acknowledge.

networks.q: What is the standard Ethernet Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) size?
networks.exp: The standard MTU for standard Ethernet frames is 1500 bytes (payload size excluding 14-byte Ethernet header and 4-byte CRC).

networks.q: Which protocol does the `ping` utility use to test network reachability?
networks.exp: `ping` operates at Layer 3 using ICMP Echo Request (Type 8) and listens for ICMP Echo Reply (Type 0).

networks.q: What is the difference between CSMA/CD and CSMA/CA?
options: CSMA/CD detects collisions (used in wired Ethernet); CSMA/CA avoids collisions with RTS/CTS (used in Wi-Fi 802.11)
networks.exp: Wired Ethernet can detect packet collisions simultaneously on the wire (CSMA/CD). Wireless radio cannot transmit and listen at the same frequency at once, so it avoids collisions using CSMA/CA.

devops.q: REST stands for:
devops.exp: REST = Representational State Transfer, an architectural style for stateless HTTP-based networked apps.

devops.q: git rebase vs git merge — rebase:
options: Rewrites history by replaying commits linearly
devops.exp: Rebase replays commits onto another branch creating a linear history; merge creates a merge commit preserving branch history.

devops.q: IaaS provides:
devops.exp: IaaS delivers virtualized infrastructure — VMs, storage, networking. Users manage OS and above. Examples: AWS EC2, Azure VMs.

devops.q: Containers vs VMs — containers:
options: Share host OS kernel, making them lighter
devops.exp: Containers share the host OS kernel — much lighter and faster to start than VMs which include a full guest OS.

devops.q: CI/CD stands for:
devops.exp: CI = Continuous Integration (auto build & test), CD = Continuous Delivery/Deployment (auto release to production).

devops.q: Docker Compose is used to:
options: Define and run multi-container Docker applications via YAML
devops.exp: Docker Compose uses docker-compose.yml to define multi-container apps (e.g., app + database + cache) and start them with one command.

devops.q: Kubernetes (K8s) primary function is:
options: Container orchestration — managing, scaling, self-healing containerized apps
devops.exp: Kubernetes automates deployment, scaling, rolling updates, and self-healing of containerized workloads across clusters.

devops.q: PaaS (Platform as a Service) provides:
options: Complete managed platform: runtime, middleware, OS — user only manages apps & data
devops.exp: PaaS (e.g., Heroku, Google App Engine, Azure App Service) provides the platform; devs only manage code and data.

devops.q: git stash is used to:
options: Temporarily save uncommitted changes without committing
devops.exp: git stash saves your working directory changes in a stack so you can switch branches without committing or losing work.

devops.q: Microservices architecture differs from monolith by:
options: Splitting application into small independent services each with its own deployment and scaling
Using a single database for all services
devops.exp: Microservices: each bounded context is an independent deployable service. Monolith: all components bundled in one deployable unit.

devops.q: In Agile Scrum, a Sprint is:
options: A time-boxed iteration (1-4 weeks) to deliver a potentially shippable increment
devops.exp: Sprint = fixed-length iteration where the team commits to a Sprint Backlog and delivers a working increment at the end.

devops.q: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) means:
options: Provisioning infrastructure (VMs, networks) via code files — e.g., Terraform, CloudFormation
devops.exp: IaC tools like Terraform declare infrastructure resources in config files — enabling version control, reproducibility, and automated provisioning.

devops.q: Which HTTP method is idempotent AND safe?
devops.exp: GET is both safe (no state change) and idempotent (same result on repeat). POST creates resources (not idempotent). PUT is idempotent but not safe.

devops.q: Blue-Green deployment strategy means:
options: Deploying on blue or green servers only
Maintaining two identical environments; switching traffic from old (blue) to new (green) for zero-downtime releases
devops.exp: Blue-Green: Blue = current production, Green = new version. After validation, route traffic to Green. Instant rollback by switching back to Blue.

devops.q: Git 'origin' refers to:
options: The default remote repository URL (e.g., GitHub)
devops.exp: 'origin' is git's default alias for the remote repository URL you cloned from or added with git remote add.

devops.q: In a Dockerfile, what is the fundamental difference between `CMD` and `ENTRYPOINT`?
options: ENTRYPOINT defines the fixed executable, while CMD provides default arguments that can be overridden at runtime
CMD runs during build, ENTRYPOINT at runtime
devops.exp: `ENTRYPOINT` sets the immutable command binary (e.g. `['python', 'app.py']`), while `CMD` supplies default parameters that CLI users can easily override via `docker run`.

devops.q: What is the primary benefit of Multi-Stage Builds in Docker?
options: Drastically reduces final production image size by leaving compilers and build tools in interim stages
devops.exp: Multi-stage builds allow developers to compile source code with heavy SDKs in stage 1, then copy only the stripped binary/artifacts into a lean production runtime image (e.g. Alpine).

devops.q: In Kubernetes, what is the smallest deployable compute unit?
options: Pod (group of one or more containers sharing network/storage)
devops.exp: A Pod is the smallest execution unit in Kubernetes; it encapsulates one or more co-located containers that share an IP address and volume storage.

devops.q: What does `git cherry-pick <commit-hash>` do?
options: Applies the changes from an individual commit onto the current working HEAD branch
devops.exp: `git cherry-pick` selects a single commit from another branch and replays its diff as a new commit onto the currently checked-out branch.

devops.q: What does a 'Detached HEAD' state indicate in Git?
options: HEAD points directly to a specific commit hash rather than a named branch ref
devops.exp: A detached HEAD means HEAD points directly to a commit SHA (e.g. after checking out a tag or specific commit); new commits made in this state won't belong to any branch unless one is created.

devops.q: What is a Canary Deployment release strategy?
options: Gradually rolling out the new release to a tiny subset of users (e.g. 5%) to verify stability before full rollout
Deploying identical code to two clusters
devops.exp: Canary deployment routes a small percentage of production traffic to the new version to detect errors with minimal blast radius before rolling out to 100% of users.

devops.q: What is the architectural role of Prometheus in cloud-native monitoring?
options: Time-series metrics database that scrapes telemetry endpoints via a pull model
devops.exp: Prometheus is a time-series monitoring system that pulls/scrapes metrics over HTTP from instrumented targets and stores them with key-value labels.

devops.q: What is the difference between a Docker Volume and a Bind Mount?
options: Volumes are slower than bind mounts
Volumes are fully managed by Docker in a dedicated storage area (`/var/lib/docker/volumes`), whereas bind mounts map to any host file path
devops.exp: Volumes are Docker-managed storage isolated from host OS specifics, making them portable and secure. Bind mounts depend on host directory hierarchies.

devops.q: According to Semantic Versioning (SemVer `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`), when must the MAJOR version increment?
devops.exp: SemVer rules: Increment MAJOR for breaking API changes, MINOR for backwards-compatible new features, and PATCH for backwards-compatible bug fixes.

devops.q: What is the primary role of a Reverse Proxy (like NGINX) in frontend architecture?
options: Fronting backend servers to handle SSL termination, load balancing, compression, and hiding internal topology
devops.exp: A reverse proxy sits in front of web servers and intercepts client requests, performing TLS termination, caching, load balancing, and preventing direct public access to internal microservices.

aptitude.q: A train 150m long passes a pole in 15 seconds. Speed of the train?
20% of a number is 80. What is 35% of that number?
Two pipes fill a tank in 12 and 15 hours. Together they take:
Boys:Girls = 3:2. Total 30 students. How many girls?
Bought at ₹200, sold at ₹250. Profit percentage?
Simple Interest on ₹5000 at 8% p.a. for 3 years?
Average of 5 numbers is 20. If one number is removed, average becomes 18. Removed number?
A person covers 60 km in 2 hours by car, then 40 km in 2 hours by foot. Average speed?
aptitude.exp: Total distance = 60 + 40 = 100 km. Total time = 2 + 2 = 4 hours. Average speed = 100 / 4 = 25 km/h.

aptitude.q: In how many ways can 5 books be arranged on a shelf?
Compound Interest on ₹10,000 at 10% p.a. compounded annually for 2 years?
Probability of getting a head in a fair coin toss?
aptitude.exp: Fair coin has 2 equally likely outcomes (H, T). P(H) = 1/2.

aptitude.q: If A can do a job in 10 days and B in 15 days, together they finish in:
The ratio 3:4 is equivalent to:
A car travels 300 km at 60 km/h and returns at 90 km/h. Average speed for round trip?
₹800 increased by 25% then decreased by 25%. Final amount?
aptitude.exp: After +25%: 800×1.25 = 1000. After −25%: 1000×0.75 = 750. Net loss due to different bases.

aptitude.q: A boat travels downstream at 14 km/h and upstream at 8 km/h. What is the speed of the boat in still water?
aptitude.exp: Speed in still water = (Downstream + Upstream) / 2 = (14 + 8) / 2 = 11 km/h. (Stream speed = (14 - 8)/2 = 3 km/h).

aptitude.q: A pipe can fill a tank in 6 hours, but due to a leak at the bottom it takes 8 hours. How long will the leak alone take to empty a full tank?
aptitude.exp: Leak rate = 1/6 - 1/8 = (4 - 3)/24 = 1/24 tank/hr. Thus, the leak alone empties the tank in 24 hours.

aptitude.q: What is the angle between the hour hand and the minute hand of a clock at 3:30?
What is the difference between Compound Interest and Simple Interest on ₹25,000 for 2 years at 8% per annum?
Two trains of lengths 120m and 180m are traveling in opposite directions at 42 km/h and 48 km/h. How many seconds will they take to cross each other completely?
aptitude.exp: Total distance = 120 + 180 = 300m. Relative speed = 42 + 48 = 90 km/h = 90 × (5/18) = 25 m/s. Time = 300 / 25 = 12 seconds.

aptitude.q: A dealer marks an article 30% above the cost price and allows a discount of 10% on the marked price. Find his profit percentage.
What is the probability of drawing either a King or a Heart from a standard deck of 52 playing cards?
aptitude.exp: P(King or Heart) = P(King) + P(Heart) - P(King of Hearts) = 4/52 + 13/52 - 1/52 = 16/52 = 4/13.

aptitude.q: In what ratio must tea at ₹62 per kg be mixed with tea at ₹72 per kg so that the mixture is worth ₹65 per kg?
A and B can do a work in 12 days and 18 days. If they work on alternate days starting with A, in how many days will the work finish?
aptitude.exp: LCM of (12, 18) = 36 units. A does 3 units/day, B does 2 units/day. In 2 days = 5 units. In 14 days (7 cycles) = 35 units done. Remaining 1 unit done by A in 1/3 day. Total = 14 + 1/3 ≈ 14.33 days.

aptitude.q: If 1st January 2024 was a Monday, what day of the week was 1st January 2025?
aptitude.exp: 2024 is a leap year (366 days = 52 weeks + 2 odd days). Adding 2 days to Monday gives Wednesday.

verbal.q: Choose the synonym of 'VERBOSE':
verbal.exp: Verbose = using too many words. Synonym = Wordy.

verbal.q: Identify the error: 'He go to school every day'
verbal.exp: 'go' should be 'goes' — third-person singular requires -s/-es in simple present.

verbal.q: Select the correctly spelled word:
verbal.exp: Correct: 'Accommodation' — double 'c' and double 'm'.

verbal.q: Antonym of 'BENEVOLENT':
verbal.exp: Benevolent = kind/well-meaning. Antonym = Malevolent (wishing evil).

verbal.q: 'She _____ to the market yesterday.'
verbal.exp: 'Yesterday' = past tense. Past of 'go' = 'went'.

verbal.q: 'The project was ___ by the team within the deadline.'
verbal.exp: Passive voice 'was ___' requires past participle 'Completed'.

verbal.q: Correct passive voice sentence:
options: The man was bitten by the dog
The man bited by the dog
The dog was biting the man
verbal.exp: Passive: Object + was/were + past participle + by agent. 'The man was bitten by the dog'.

verbal.q: 'The wind whispered through the trees' is an example of:
verbal.exp: Personification attributes human quality (whispering) to non-human entity (wind).

verbal.q: Choose the word: 'Despite working _____, she finished on time.'
verbal.exp: 'Despite' + positive result (finished on time) suggests hard work = 'diligently'.

verbal.q:
Para jumble: Which sequence makes a coherent paragraph?
A: She loved reading.
B: Books were her escape.
C: Every evening she read.
D: Libraries were her sanctuary.
verbal.exp: Logical sequence A-B-D-C.

verbal.q: Idiom meaning: 'Bite the bullet'
options: To endure a painful situation with courage
verbal.exp: 'Bite the bullet' means to face a difficult situation with bravery.

verbal.q: Find the error: 'Neither of the two candidates have submitted their resume.'
verbal.exp: 'Neither of' takes a singular verb: 'has submitted'.

verbal.q: Choose antonym of 'EPHEMERAL':
verbal.exp: Ephemeral = temporary. Antonym = Eternal/Permanent.

verbal.q: Sentence Improvement: 'I look forward to meet you.'
verbal.exp: 'Look forward to' takes a gerund (-ing): 'to meeting you'.

verbal.q: Synonym of 'PRAGMATIC':
verbal.exp: Pragmatic means practical, dealing with things realistically.

verbal.q: Select the synonym of 'UBIQUITOUS':
verbal.exp: Ubiquitous means present, appearing, or found everywhere (e.g. 'Smartphones have become ubiquitous').

verbal.q: Select the synonym of 'METICULOUS':
verbal.exp: Meticulous refers to showing great attention to detail, very careful and precise.

verbal.q: Choose the antonym of 'CANDOR':
verbal.exp: Candor means being open, honest, and frank. The antonym is deceitfulness, insincerity, or guile.

verbal.q: Choose the antonym of 'PLACATE':
verbal.exp: To placate means to make someone less angry or hostile. The opposite is to enrage or provoke.

verbal.q: Identify the error: 'Scarcely had the teacher entered the classroom then the students stood up.'
verbal.exp: 'Scarcely' and 'Hardly' are always paired with 'when', not 'then' (e.g. 'Scarcely had... when...').

verbal.q: Fill in the blank: 'The committee _____ divided in their opinions regarding the budget.'
verbal.exp: When a collective noun functions with members acting individually or with differing opinions, it takes a plural verb ('were divided').

verbal.q: Choose the correct preposition: 'She has been working in this firm _____ 2021.'
verbal.exp: 'Since' is used to denote a specific starting point in time in the past for actions continuing into the present.

verbal.q: What is the meaning of the idiom 'To spill the beans'?
options: To disclose a secret prematurely or inadvertently
verbal.exp: 'To spill the beans' means to reveal secret information accidentally or maliciously.

verbal.q: What is the meaning of the idiom 'To burn the midnight oil'?
options: To work or study late into the night
verbal.exp: 'To burn the midnight oil' means to work or study late into the night.

verbal.q: Convert to Indirect Speech: He said, 'I have completed my assignment.'
options: He said that he completed his assignment.
He said that he had completed his assignment.
He said that he has completed his assignment.
He said that he would complete his assignment.
verbal.exp: Present Perfect ('have completed') shifts to Past Perfect ('had completed') in reported speech with a past reporting verb.

verbal.q: Choose the correct passive voice: 'They will announce the results tomorrow.'
options: The results will be announced tomorrow by them.
The results have been announced tomorrow.
verbal.exp: Simple Future passive voice structure: Subject + will + be + past participle ('will be announced').

verbal.q: Select the correctly spelled word:
verbal.exp: Correct spelling is 'Bureaucracy' (b-u-r-e-a-u-c-r-a-c-y).

verbal.q: One Word Substitution: 'A person who hates or distrusts humankind'
verbal.exp: A misanthrope is someone who dislikes, distrusts, or avoids human society.

verbal.q: Identify the correct sentence:
options: One of the students who has participated is absent.
One of the students who have participated is absent.
One of the student who has participated is absent.
One of the students who have participated are absent.
verbal.exp: The relative pronoun 'who' refers to plural antecedent 'students' (taking 'have participated'), while the main clause subject 'One' takes singular verb 'is absent'.

verbal.q: What does the idiom 'Cut corners' mean?
options: To do something poorly or cheaply in order to save time or money
verbal.exp: 'To cut corners' means to undertake a task in the easiest, cheapest, or fastest way, frequently compromising quality.

Find the bug in Binary Search midpoint calculation:
int mid = (low + high) / 2;
options: Causes integer overflow if low + high exceeds INT_MAX; should be low + (high - low) / 2
debugging.exp: For large array indices (e.g. low + high > 2^31 - 1), direct addition wraps into negative numbers causing an overflow crash. Use `low + (high - low) / 2`.

double cannot be multiplied by int
debugging.exp: 0.1 cannot be represented exactly in binary floating-point. Comparing with `==` often fails. Always compare with an epsilon tolerance.

debugging.exp: `*ptr++` evaluates to `*(ptr++)`, advancing the pointer to the next element. If the intent was incrementing the integer value, parentheses are required: `(*ptr)++`.

Variable-length arrays are strictly forbidden in all compilers
debugging.exp: Standard 2D DP problems (like LCS or Edit Distance) require index 0 as an empty string/base case, requiring an array of dimensions `(m+1) × (n+1)`.

str is not a char pointer
